subtopic_detail: Three weeks of vomiting at nine weeks with a 3 per cent weight loss in a woman still tolerating some oral fluid
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a 26 year old woman at nine weeks in her first pregnancy who has been vomiting for three weeks. She vomits four or five times a day, mostly in the mornings, and feels nauseated for much of the rest of the day.

She has been eating dry crackers before getting up, taking small frequent meals and using ginger tablets for a fortnight without much benefit. She is still able to keep down about a litre of fluid a day and has not vomited blood. She weighed 62 kg before the pregnancy and weighs 60 kg today. She has no abdominal pain, no fever, no urinary symptoms and no diarrhoea. Her thyroid is not enlarged and she has no tremor or lid lag. Her urine dipstick shows ketones at one plus with no nitrites or leucocytes, and her thyroid stimulating hormone is 0.09 mIU/L with a normal free thyroxine. An ultrasound this morning confirmed a single intrauterine pregnancy with a normal heartbeat.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88 per minute, blood pressure 108/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 99 per cent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Urine dipstick ketones one plus with no nitrites or leucocytes, thyroid stimulating hormone 0.09 mIU/L (0.4-4.0) with free thyroxine within normal limits, sodium 137 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 3.8 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine within normal limits
data_table.Imaging: Transvaginal ultrasound showing a single intrauterine pregnancy with foetal heart activity and no molar features

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her management?

options.text: Admit her for intravenous rehydration and intravenous antiemetics today
options.rationale: Admission is indicated when a woman cannot maintain oral hydration, has lost more than 5 per cent of body weight, or has electrolyte disturbance or ketosis with clinical dehydration, and she is tolerating a litre a day with normal electrolytes. Admitting first also skips the oral step that resolves most cases (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start ondansetron 4 mg orally as required and review her in one week
options.rationale: Ondansetron is effective but is positioned as a second or third line agent in Australian practice because of a small absolute increase in orofacial clefting reported with first trimester exposure, so it is used after the first line combination has failed. The counselling that goes with it is unnecessary if the earlier step works (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start oral doxylamine with pyridoxine and review her in one week
options.rationale: This combination has the longest safety record of any antiemetic in pregnancy and is first line once non pharmacological measures have failed, which they have after a fortnight of ginger and dietary change. Her weight loss of 3 per cent with tolerated oral intake and normal electrolytes places her in the moderate category managed as an outpatient (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start prednisolone 40 mg orally daily and taper over the next fortnight
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are a last resort for refractory hyperemesis after multiple agents have failed and are avoided before ten weeks because of a reported association with orofacial clefting. Starting them before any antiemetic has been trialled inverts the ladder (Source: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy

options.text: Start carbimazole for her suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone level
options.rationale: A suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine in the first trimester reflects cross stimulation of the thyroid receptor by human chorionic gonadotrophin and resolves as levels fall after about twelve weeks. Treating it would produce iatrogenic hypothyroidism in a euthyroid woman (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy).
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

explanation.summary: Nausea and vomiting affects around 70 to 80 per cent of pregnancies, typically beginning before nine weeks and settling by sixteen to twenty weeks, and severity is best graded with a validated score such as the Pregnancy Unique Quantification of Emesis alongside weight loss and ketosis. Hyperemesis gravidarum is the severe end and is defined by persistent vomiting with weight loss over 5 per cent, dehydration and electrolyte or acid base disturbance. Management is stepwise, beginning with dietary and lifestyle measures, then doxylamine with pyridoxine, then metoclopramide or prochlorperazine, then ondansetron, with corticosteroids reserved for refractory disease. Transient gestational thyrotoxicosis is common and needs no treatment because it reflects the structural similarity between human chorionic gonadotrophin and thyroid stimulating hormone. Women admitted for rehydration need thiamine before any dextrose containing fluid to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy, and this is the most consequential omission in the condition.
key_points: Grade severity by weight loss, ability to tolerate fluids, ketosis and electrolytes
Doxylamine with pyridoxine is the first line pharmacological treatment
Ondansetron is second or third line in Australia because of a small clefting signal
A suppressed thyroid stimulating hormone with normal free thyroxine needs no treatment
Weight loss beyond 5 per cent with dehydration indicates admission
explanation.pearls: Give thiamine before any dextrose containing intravenous fluid to a woman admitted with prolonged vomiting in pregnancy, because glucose loading a thiamine depleted woman can precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy within hours.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Nausea and vomiting of pregnancy
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Nausea and vomiting in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Fourteen months of preoccupation with a neurological diagnosis despite three normal specialist reviews, with almost no bodily symptoms
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 39 year old accountant referred by his general practitioner. For fourteen months he has been convinced he is developing motor neurone disease, which began when a colleague of a similar age was diagnosed with it.

He checks his tongue in the bathroom mirror for twitching several times a day, tests his grip strength on a door handle each morning, and spends around two hours most evenings reading patient forums. He has been reviewed by three neurologists, and MRI of his brain and cervical spine, nerve conduction studies and electromyography have all been normal. He tells you each normal result settles him for about two days before the worry returns, and that he now avoids opening the results letters. His only bodily symptom is occasional twitching of his calf muscles after exercise, which he does not find painful or limiting. His mood is reactive, he continues to work and exercise, and he scores 6 on the Patient Health Questionnaire 9.

data_table.Examination: Normal cranial nerve, motor, sensory and reflex examination, no fasciculation observed, no muscle wasting, normal gait, reactive affect with no psychomotor change
data_table.Investigations: MRI brain and cervical spine, nerve conduction studies and electromyography all reported as normal, Patient Health Questionnaire 9 score 6 out of 27, creatine kinase and thyroid function within normal limits
data_table.Behaviour: Checks tongue and grip several times daily, approximately two hours each evening reading health forums, avoids opening results letters

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Repeat the MRI of his brain and cervical spine for definitive reassurance
options.rationale: Repeated investigation is the central maintaining factor in this condition because each normal result provides relief that lasts days and then strengthens the need for the next test. Reassurance seeking is the behaviour being treated, not the treatment (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

options.text: Arrange a fourth neurology opinion at a different hospital for certainty
options.rationale: Another specialist opinion repeats the same reassurance cycle at greater cost and reinforces the belief that the previous assessments may have missed something. It differs from repeat imaging only in the form the reassurance takes (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

options.text: Start diazepam as required for when the worry about his health peaks
options.rationale: A short acting benzodiazepine taken at peaks of anxiety functions as a safety behaviour that prevents the natural extinction of the anxiety, and it carries tolerance and dependence risk over a fourteen month problem. Where medication is used in this condition it is a serotonin reuptake inhibitor taken regularly (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic).

options.text: Refer him for cognitive behavioural therapy and arrange regular scheduled review
options.rationale: Cognitive behavioural therapy targeting catastrophic misinterpretation of bodily sensations, checking and reassurance seeking has the strongest evidence in this disorder, with effects sustained at follow up. Scheduling appointments at fixed intervals rather than in response to symptoms breaks the link between worry and medical contact, which is the behavioural half of the treatment (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

options.text: Advise him to stop searching online and review him only if symptoms change
options.rationale: Advice to stop checking without a structured programme rarely succeeds, and reviewing only when symptoms change makes medical contact contingent on symptoms, which rewards symptom focus. Fixed interval review does the opposite (Source: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders).
source_refs: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

explanation.summary: Illness anxiety disorder is characterised by preoccupation with having or acquiring a serious illness for at least six months, with somatic symptoms that are absent or mild, high health anxiety and either excessive health related behaviours or maladaptive avoidance. It is distinguished from somatic symptom disorder, in which distressing physical symptoms are prominent, and the DSM-5 revision split the former diagnosis of hypochondriasis along exactly this line. The disorder is maintained by a cycle of bodily attention, catastrophic interpretation, checking and reassurance seeking, in which each normal result gives short lived relief and increases the need for the next. Care and avoidance seeking subtypes both occur, and the avoidant subtype can present late with genuine pathology missed through avoidance of medical contact. Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, a serotonin reuptake inhibitor is an effective alternative or addition, and the single most useful structural change is moving to appointments at fixed intervals with one consistent doctor.
key_points: Preoccupation with illness for six months with minimal somatic symptoms defines the diagnosis
Reassurance relieves anxiety briefly and then strengthens the cycle
Cognitive behavioural therapy is first line, with a serotonin reuptake inhibitor as an alternative
Scheduled rather than symptom triggered review breaks the reinforcement pattern
The avoidant subtype risks genuine pathology being missed
explanation.pearls: Set appointments at fixed intervals such as every four weeks regardless of symptoms, and agree in advance that new investigations require a new objective sign rather than a new worry, because this single arrangement reduces both consultations and investigation rates substantially.

sources.label: RANZCP: Somatic symptom and related disorders

subtopic_detail: Nausea, confusion and yellow tinged vision in an elderly woman whose diuretic dose was increased after a heart failure admission
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing an 81 year old woman brought in by her daughter with four days of nausea, poor appetite and confusion. She has permanent atrial fibrillation and has taken digoxin 125 mcg daily for six years, along with apixaban and perindopril.

Her daughter says that after an admission for heart failure three weeks ago her frusemide was increased from 40 mg to 80 mg daily, and that since then her mother has been complaining that the kitchen lights look yellow and have halos around them. She has not fallen, has no chest pain and has no fever, cough or dysuria. On examination she is drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only, with dry mucous membranes and no focal neurological signs. Her chest is clear and her jugular venous pressure is not elevated. Her electrocardiogram shows atrial fibrillation at a ventricular rate of 44 per minute with downsloping ST depression in the lateral leads and no ventricular ectopy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 44 per minute, blood pressure 106/62 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 per minute, SpO2 96 per cent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Investigations: Serum digoxin 3.4 nmol/L (1.0-2.6), potassium 3.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), creatinine 155 micromol/L (45-90, baseline 90), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), corrected calcium within normal limits, troponin within normal limits
data_table.Electrocardiogram: Atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 44 per minute, downsloping lateral ST depression, no ventricular ectopy or ventricular tachycardia

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Withhold digoxin and correct her potassium with careful replacement
options.rationale: Stopping the drug and correcting the hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia that potentiate its effect on the sodium potassium pump treats both the toxicity and the reason it developed, alongside withholding the diuretic and rehydrating to restore renal clearance. She has no life threatening arrhythmia and a potassium of 3.1 mmol/L, so this conservative approach with continuous monitoring is appropriate (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give digoxin specific antibody fragments as an intravenous infusion now
options.rationale: Antibody fragments are reserved for life threatening ventricular arrhythmia, haemodynamically significant bradycardia unresponsive to atropine, a potassium above about 5.0 to 5.5 mmol/L in acute poisoning, or a large acute ingestion, none of which applies here. Her hypokalaemia in fact argues that the toxicity is chronic and less immediately dangerous (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Insert a temporary transvenous pacing wire for her slow heart rate
options.rationale: Temporary pacing in this setting is associated with provoking ventricular arrhythmias in a myocardium already sensitised by the drug, and it is used only when bradycardia causes haemodynamic compromise unresponsive to atropine and antibody fragments. Her blood pressure of 106/62 mmHg does not meet that bar (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and toxinology).

options.text: Give intravenous calcium chloride to stabilise the cardiac membrane
options.rationale: Calcium is the standard membrane stabilising treatment for hyperkalaemia, but it is traditionally avoided in this poisoning because the drug already raises intracellular calcium and further loading has been linked to refractory contracture. She is hypokalaemic in any case, so there is no hyperkalaemia to treat (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

options.text: Halve the digoxin dose and recheck her digoxin level in one week
options.rationale: Continuing any dose while the level is above the therapeutic range and renal clearance is impaired allows further accumulation, and a week is far too long an interval for a confused bradycardic patient. Dose reduction becomes the discussion once the level and renal function have normalised (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).

explanation.summary: Chronic digoxin toxicity is typically precipitated by a change in renal function, volume status or an interacting drug rather than by a dose change, and diuretic escalation causes both dehydration with reduced clearance and the hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia that increase myocardial sensitivity. Presentation is with nausea, anorexia, confusion and visual disturbance described as yellow or green tinged vision with halos, together with bradyarrhythmias, atrioventricular block or ventricular ectopy. The downsloping ST depression often called the reverse tick is an effect of the drug at therapeutic levels and does not itself indicate toxicity. Serum levels correlate poorly with toxicity in chronic poisoning, so treatment is driven by the clinical picture and the electrocardiogram rather than the number. Amiodarone, verapamil, macrolides and spironolactone all raise digoxin levels and are worth reviewing whenever a level rises unexpectedly.
key_points: Renal impairment, dehydration, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia precipitate chronic toxicity
Yellow or green tinged vision with halos is the characteristic visual symptom
Antibody fragments are for life threatening arrhythmia, refractory bradycardia or hyperkalaemia
In acute poisoning a high potassium predicts mortality, whereas chronic toxicity is often hypokalaemic
Levels correlate poorly with toxicity in chronic poisoning and do not drive treatment alone
explanation.pearls: Correct magnesium as well as potassium, because hypomagnesaemia both causes refractory hypokalaemia and independently sensitises the myocardium, and potassium replacement alone will keep failing until the magnesium is replaced.

subtopic_detail: A long narrow head with a palpable ridge in a five month old whose ears are symmetrical and whose head circumference is tracking normally
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a five month old boy referred by his maternal child health nurse because of his head shape. His parents say his head has looked long and narrow since about six weeks of age and that it has not changed with the repositioning advice they were given.

He was born at term by normal vaginal birth and was not a twin, he has never had a preference for turning one way, and he tolerates tummy time well. On examination, looking down at his head from above, it is long from front to back and narrow from side to side, with a prominent forehead and a pointed occiput, and both ears sit level with each other and are not pushed forward on either side. Running your fingers along the midline of the skull you feel a firm raised ridge extending from the anterior fontanelle backwards. The anterior fontanelle is small but patent and soft. His head circumference is on the 75th centile and has tracked there since birth, and his development and neurological examination are normal.

data_table.Examination: Vertex view shows an elongated narrow skull with frontal prominence and occipital pointing, ears symmetrically positioned, firm palpable midline sagittal ridge, anterior fontanelle small and soft, no facial asymmetry, normal tone power and reflexes
data_table.Growth: Head circumference on the 75th centile tracking consistently since birth, weight and length on the 50th centile

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Advise repositioning and tummy time and review his head shape in three months
options.rationale: Repositioning treats deformation from external pressure, which produces a parallelogram shaped head with the ear and forehead on the flattened side pushed forward, and it cannot alter a skull constrained by a fused suture. A further three months also passes through the period of most rapid brain growth when surgical correction is most effective (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Refer him to a paediatric craniofacial service for urgent assessment
options.rationale: A boat shaped skull that is long and narrow with a palpable midline ridge and symmetrical ears indicates premature fusion of the sagittal suture rather than positional moulding, and the diagnosis is confirmed and managed in a specialist unit. Referral is time critical because minimally invasive endoscopic techniques are generally restricted to infants under about six months, after which open cranial vault remodelling is required (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Refer him for a moulding helmet to be fitted over the next month
options.rationale: Helmet therapy reshapes a skull whose sutures are all open by directing growth away from the prominent areas, and it has no capacity to release a fused suture. It differs from the correct option in treating the shape rather than the constraint that produces it (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is a normal variant of head shape
options.rationale: A palpable ridge over a suture with a skull shape that has not responded to repositioning is not a normal variant, and untreated single suture fusion can lead to raised intracranial pressure in a minority as well as a permanent cosmetic deformity. A normal head circumference is expected because compensatory growth occurs along the unfused sutures (Source: RCH CPG: Abnormal head shape).

options.text: Arrange a cranial ultrasound to assess the ventricles and sutures
options.rationale: Ultrasound through the fontanelle images the brain rather than defining suture fusion and would delay referral without changing the answer. Where imaging is used it is a low dose computed tomogram with three dimensional reconstruction, arranged by the receiving unit (Source: Royal Children's Hospital: Craniosynostosis).

explanation.summary: Abnormal head shape in infancy is usually positional in origin and follows the rise in supine sleeping, producing a flattened occiput with the ipsilateral ear and forehead displaced forward, giving a parallelogram when viewed from above. Craniosynostosis is far less common at about one in two thousand births and produces a characteristic shape determined by which suture has fused, with growth restricted perpendicular to the fused suture and compensatory growth parallel to it. Sagittal synostosis is the commonest single suture form and produces a long narrow skull with frontal bossing and occipital pointing, with symmetrical ear position and often a palpable ridge. Head circumference is typically normal in single suture disease because compensatory growth preserves volume, so a normal measurement is not reassuring. Multi suture and syndromic forms, including Apert and Crouzon syndromes, carry a much higher risk of raised intracranial pressure and are managed in specialist craniofacial units.
key_points: Positional moulding gives a parallelogram with the ear displaced forward on the flat side
Synostosis gives a shape determined by which suture is fused, with symmetrical ears
A palpable ridge over a suture is a key discriminating sign
Head circumference is usually normal in single suture synostosis
Endoscopic correction is generally limited to infants under about six months of age
explanation.pearls: Look at the head from directly above rather than from the front, because the parallelogram of positional moulding and the elongated boat shape of sagittal synostosis are almost indistinguishable face to face and unmistakable from the vertex view.

subtopic_detail: A doctor consulting you as her own general practitioner who describes starting operating lists still affected by the previous night's drinking
stem:
You are the general practice registrar at a practice in regional Victoria seeing a 44 year old woman who has been your patient for two years. She is an anaesthetist at the local hospital and has come asking for a repeat prescription of oxycodone for chronic back pain.

The real time prescription monitoring system alerts you that she has received oxycodone prescriptions from two other practices in the past six weeks. When you raise this she becomes tearful and tells you that her marriage has ended, that she has been drinking most of a bottle of spirits most nights to get to sleep, and that on two recent mornings she began her operating list still feeling affected by the previous night's drinking. She says her list starts at eight and she has not had any adverse patient outcomes. She asks you not to tell anyone because she is worried she will lose her registration and her income, and she agrees to see an addiction specialist next week.

data_table.Examination: Tearful but oriented and cooperative, no tremor or sweating at this consultation, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, no injection marks
data_table.Investigations: Gamma glutamyl transferase 148 U/L (5-35), mean cell volume 99 fL (80-98), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 35), full blood count otherwise within normal limits
data_table.Prescription monitoring: Oxycodone dispensed from three prescribers across two other practices within the past six weeks

lead_in: What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.text: Maintain confidentiality, treat her alcohol use and review her again next week
options.rationale: Confidentiality is not absolute and yields where a practitioner has practised while intoxicated, because the risk transfers to patients who cannot consent to it. Treating her is necessary but is not an alternative to the notification (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

options.text: Refer her to the doctors health advisory service instead of notifying anyone
options.rationale: Doctors health services are a valuable support and should be offered, but referral to them does not discharge a mandatory obligation once the practitioner has practised while intoxicated. They are the complement to the notification rather than a substitute for it (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

options.text: Tell her head of department about your concerns and leave the decision to them
options.rationale: Delegating the judgement to an employer does not satisfy a personal statutory obligation that rests with the practitioner who forms the reasonable belief, and it discloses her health information to a party with no clinical role. Employers have their own separate notification duties (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

options.text: Decline to continue as her doctor and advise her to see someone else
options.rationale: Withdrawing care removes the one therapeutic relationship she has disclosed to, makes future help seeking less likely and still leaves the obligation unmet. Practitioner patients are entitled to the same continuity of care as anyone else (Source: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice).
source_refs: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice

options.text: Make a mandatory notification to the regulator and continue to treat her
options.rationale: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is one of the four forms of notifiable conduct under the National Law, and her account of starting operating lists still affected meets that threshold irrespective of whether any patient has been harmed. Treating practitioners in Victoria are not exempt, and the notification is made while the therapeutic relationship continues, with an explanation to her of what you must do and why (Source: Ahpra: Guidelines for mandatory notifications).

explanation.summary: Notifiable conduct under the Health Practitioner Regulation National Law comprises practising while intoxicated by alcohol or drugs, sexual misconduct in the course of practice, placing the public at substantial risk of harm through practice that departs significantly from accepted standards, and placing the public at substantial risk of harm by practising with an impairment. The 2020 reforms deliberately raised the threshold for treating practitioners for the impairment and standards limbs to substantial risk of harm, in order to encourage doctors to seek health care, but the intoxication and sexual misconduct limbs were not softened. Western Australia exempts treating practitioners from mandatory notification altogether and Queensland has its own variation, so jurisdiction matters. An impairment that is being appropriately treated and is not placing patients at substantial risk does not require notification, which is the point most often misunderstood. Doctors health advisory services operate in every state and territory and offer confidential assessment, and referral to them sits alongside rather than instead of any obligation that has been triggered.
key_points: Practising while intoxicated by alcohol is notifiable conduct with no softened threshold
The 2020 reforms raised the treating practitioner threshold only for the impairment and standards limbs
Western Australia exempts treating practitioners entirely and Queensland differs
An impairment under appropriate treatment without substantial risk is not notifiable
Notification and continuing to provide care are not alternatives
explanation.pearls: Tell the practitioner patient in the consultation that you are required to notify and why, because doing so preserves the therapeutic relationship far more often than a notification they learn about later from the regulator.

sources.label: Medical Board of Australia: Good medical practice
